front: What is a process?
back: An instance of an executing program. The terms task and job are often used interchangeably with process.

front: How does an application on disk differ from a process?
back: On disk an application is static. Once launched it is loaded into memory and starts executing, becoming a process, which is an active entity.

front: If the same program is launched more than once, what results?
back: Multiple processes are created. They have the same instructions but very different state.

front: Does a process have to be running at every moment to be a process?
back: No. A process represents the execution state of an active application; it may be waiting on user input or waiting for another process that holds the CPU.

front: What state does a process encapsulate?
back: All the state of a running application: the code, the data, the heap, and the stack.
source: What Does a Process Look Like?

front: What OS abstraction encapsulates all of the process state, uniquely identified by address?
back: An address space, defined by a range of addresses V_0 to V_max.
source: What Does a Process Look Like?

front: Address space: what does the data region hold, as opposed to the heap?
back: The static state available when the process is first initialized. The heap holds dynamically created state (memory the process allocates, intermediate results, data read from files).
source: What Does a Process Look Like?

text: In the address space, the heap holds dynamically created state, while the stack holds dynamically created state that {{c1::grows and shrinks}} as the program executes.
source: What Does a Process Look Like?

front: The heap is drawn as a contiguous region, but in reality what does it contain?
back: It may have holes: regions that have no meaning for the process and that the process is not permitted to access. The OS tracks which addresses are valid.
source: What Does a Process Look Like?

front: What ordering discipline does the stack follow, and how does it change?
back: LIFO. Stack frames are added and removed as functions are called and return.
source: What Does a Process Look Like?

front: When a process calls procedure y, what happens to its prior state?
back: The state before the call is pushed onto the stack and control jumps to y. When y returns, that state is popped off and execution continues exactly as before.
source: What Does a Process Look Like?

front: Show the layout of a process address space (code, data, heap, stack).
source: What Does a Process Look Like?

front: Process address space: what are the addresses from V_0 to V_max called, and why?
back: Virtual addresses. They are virtual because they do not have to correspond to actual locations in physical memory.

front: What is the benefit of mapping virtual addresses to physical addresses?
back: It decouples the layout of data in the virtual address space from the layout of data in physical memory, so the virtual layout does not constrain how physical memory is managed.

front: What maintains the mapping between virtual and physical addresses?
back: Memory management hardware and components of the OS.

text: The OS mapping between a process's virtual addresses and physical addresses is called a {{c1::page table}}.

front: Address space and memory management: give two reasons the full V_0 to V_max range may not reside in physical memory.
back:
• Parts of the address space may simply be unallocated.
  • There may not be enough physical memory to store all the state even when needed.

front: How much can a single address space span with 32-bit virtual addresses?
back: Up to 4GB. Running several such processes at once exhausts physical memory quickly even on a well-provisioned machine.

front: How does the OS handle more address-space state than physical memory can hold?
back: It dynamically decides which portion lives in physical memory and which is swapped to disk. Swapped-out regions are brought back when needed, which may force other regions out to make room.

front: Beyond maintaining the virtual-to-physical mapping, what must the OS check on memory accesses?
back: The validity of accesses, e.g. ensuring process A is not writing to memory mapped by process B.

front: Can two processes running at the same time have the exact same virtual address range (e.g. 0 to 64,000)?
back: Yes. Virtual addresses are decoupled from physical addresses, so the OS maps P1's virtual addresses to one set of physical locations and P2's to another. Identical virtual ranges still resolve to distinct physical memory.

front: Why must the OS know what a process is doing when it stops it?
back: So it can resume execution with the exact same state the process had when it was stopped.

front: Are a binary's instructions executed strictly in order?
back: No. Jumps, loops, and interrupts redirect the flow.

front: What is the program counter?
back: The CPU's knowledge of the current executing line within a program, i.e. where in the code a process currently is.

front: Where is the program counter maintained during execution?
back: On a CPU register. Other process state (data addresses, status information) is also stored on CPU registers.

front: What defines the top of the stack?
back: The stack pointer.

front: What is a process control block (PCB)?
back: A data structure the OS maintains for every process it manages, holding all the useful information about that process.

front: List the main contents of a PCB.
back:
• process state
  • process number
  • program counter
  • CPU registers
  • memory limits plus virtual-to-physical mappings
  • CPU scheduling info (time run, future time, priority)
  • list of open files
  • and more

front: When is a PCB created and initialized?
back: When the process is initially created. For example, the program counter is set to point at the very first instruction.

front: Give an example of a PCB field updated when process state changes.
back: Virtual/physical memory mappings may be updated when the process requests more memory.

front: How is the fast-changing program counter kept up to date without wasting time?
back: The CPU maintains a dedicated register for the program counter and automatically updates it on every new instruction.

front: Whose job is it to save a process's register data to the PCB, and when?
back: The operating system collects the data from CPU registers and saves it to the PCB when the process is no longer running.

front: Where is a PCB stored while a process is not running, and what happens when it resumes?
back: It is stored in memory. When the process starts/resumes, its PCB is loaded from memory into CPU registers, then instruction execution begins.

front: P1 is running and the OS switches to P2. Trace the PCB operations.
back:
1. Save P1's register values into P1's PCB.
  2. Restore P2's PCB into the CPU registers.
  3. P2 runs.

front: If P2 calls malloc while running, what does the OS do to its PCB?
back: It allocates the memory, establishes new virtual-to-physical mappings for P2, and updates P2's PCB accordingly.

front: When the OS restores P1's PCB after P2, where does P1 resume?
back: At the exact instruction where it left off, because the restored values are those captured when P1 was interrupted.

front: Illustrate a context switch between two processes using their PCBs.
What is a context switch?
back: A mechanism the OS uses to switch from the context of one process to the context of another process. It is expensive.

front: What are the direct costs of a context switch?
back: The number of CPU cycles required to load and store a new PCB to and from memory.

front: What are the indirect costs of a context switch?
back: Loss of a hot cache. The incoming process's data replaces the old process's cached data, so the next time the old process runs its cache is cold and the CPU spends many more cycles fetching from memory.

text: Accessing data from cache takes on the order of {{c1::cycles}}, while accessing data from memory takes on the order of {{c2::hundreds of cycles}}.

front: What does it mean for a cache to be hot vs cold?
back: Hot: the data a process needs is present and accesses resolve in cache hits. Cold: the data is not in the cache and the CPU must fetch from memory.

front: Describe the cache hierarchy mentioned for context switches.
back: There is a hierarchy: L1, L2, down to the last level cache. Each level is larger and potentially slower than the one before, but all are far faster than memory.

front: Given context-switch costs, what is the general guidance?
back: Limit how often we context switch.

front: Does a hot cache keep a process on the CPU?
back: No. We may still context switch away from a hot cache, e.g. a higher-priority process needs to run, or a timesharing policy's timeslice has expired.

front: Hot cache quiz: which options correctly complete "When a cache is hot..."? (1) it can malfunction, so we must context switch to another process; (2) most process data is in the cache, so the process performance will be at its best; (3) sometimes we must context switch.
back: Option 2 is the most correct, and option 3 is correct as well: a hot cache does not keep a process on the CPU. Option 1 is wrong; "hot" has nothing to do with physical temperature, only with accesses resolving in cache hits.

front: Process life cycle: what happens in the new state?
back: The OS performs admission control and allocates/initializes the PCB and some initial resources, provided minimum resources are available. The process then moves to ready.

front: Process life cycle: what is the ready state?
back: The process is ready to execute but is not currently executing, waiting for the scheduler to put it on the CPU.

front: Process life cycle: how does a process leave the running state?
back:
• Interrupted / context switched out, returning to ready.
  • Needs I/O or must wait on an event, entering waiting.
  • Exits (with or without error), becoming terminated.

front: Process life cycle: from the waiting state, where does a process go, and when?
back: Back to ready, when the I/O operation completes or the event occurs.

text: The process life cycle states are: {{c1::new}}, {{c2::ready}}, {{c3::running}}, {{c4::waiting}}, and {{c5::terminated}}.

front: Which process states can the CPU execute, and how do they differ?
back: Running and ready. A running process is already executing; a ready process is only waiting for the scheduler to place it on the CPU.

front: When a ready process is scheduled onto the CPU, from where does it resume?
back: From the instruction its program counter points to: the first instruction if it was newly created, or wherever it was last interrupted (by the scheduler, or because it had to wait on I/O or an event).

front: Process creation: define parent and child, and the overall structure of loaded processes.
back: A process can create child processes; the creator is the parent. All currently loaded processes form a tree-like hierarchy.

front: After the OS boots, what processes does it create, and what access do they have?
back: Some root processes, which have privileged access.

front: How is a process created when a user runs a shell command?
back: When a user logs in a shell process is created; when the user types a command, a new process is spawned as a child of that shell.

front: On UNIX-based systems, what is the parent of all user-level processes?
back: init, the first process to start after boot. Every other user-level process can be traced back to it.

front: On Android, what is the parent of all app processes, and how are apps created?
back: Zygote, a daemon that preloads the Android framework classes. Each new app process is created by forking Zygote, inheriting the preloaded framework.

front: What are the two mechanisms most operating systems support for process creation?
back: fork and exec.

front: What does fork do?
back: Creates a new PCB for the child and copies the exact values from the parent PCB into it. Both processes continue at the instruction immediately following the fork with the same program counter.

front: What does exec do?
back: Takes a PCB (created via fork) and loads a new program into it, so the child's PCB points to the new program's values and its program counter points to the new program's first instruction.

front: To create and run a new program, how are fork and exec combined?
back: Call fork to produce the process, then exec to replace the forked image with the new program's image.

front: Which OS component decides which ready process runs next on the CPU?
back: The CPU scheduler. It manages how processes use CPU resources, choosing which process runs next and for how long.

front: Define preempt / preemption in the scheduling context.
back: To interrupt the current process and save its context so another can run.

text: To run a process the OS must {{c1::preempt}} the current one and save its context, {{c2::schedule}} (select) the next process, and {{c3::dispatch}} it by switching into its context.

front: Where should the OS spend the bulk of its time, and why does scheduler efficiency matter?
back: Running processes, not making scheduling decisions. Because CPU resources are precious, scheduling algorithms and their data structures need efficient designs and implementations.

front: What information do scheduler data structures hold about waiting processes?
back: The waiting processes plus whatever feeds the scheduling decision, such as priorities and execution history.

front: CPU efficiency formula: what does T_p denote, and what is that time called?
back: The time allocated to a scheduled process, the time that process can consume on the CPU. It is known as the timeslice.

front: How is CPU efficiency measured with respect to scheduling?
back: Time spent executing a process divided by the total interval, which includes the time spent scheduling.

front: Length of process: write the CPU efficiency formula over an interval with two execution and two scheduling blocks.
back: 2 * T_p / (2 * T_p + 2 * T_sched)

front: If execution blocks and scheduling blocks are equal in number and length, what is CPU efficiency?
back: Only 50%.

front: If a process runs for 10x the length of a scheduling block (equal counts), what is CPU efficiency?
back: Roughly 91%.

front: What two design decisions must a scheduler make regarding process length?
back:
• What are appropriate timeslice values?
  • What criteria decide which process runs next?

front: What happens when a process makes an I/O request?
back: The OS delivers the request and moves the process to the I/O queue for that device. The process stays there until the device responds, then returns to the ready state. If nothing is waiting ahead of it in the ready queue, it might be scheduled on the CPU immediately.

front: List the four ways a process can end up on the ready queue.
back:
1. It was waiting on an I/O event that completed.
  2. It was running and its timeslice expired.
  3. It was newly created via fork.
  4. It was waiting for an interrupt and the interrupt occurred.

front: Diagram the flow of processes among the CPU, ready queue, and I/O queues.

Of these four, which are NOT the CPU scheduler's responsibility: maintaining the I/O queue, maintaining the ready queue, deciding when to context switch, deciding when to generate an event a process is waiting on?
back: Not the scheduler's: maintaining the I/O queue and deciding when to generate the event a process is waiting on; the scheduler has no control over when I/O or external events occur, other than the timer interrupt. The scheduler's own jobs are maintaining the ready queue and deciding when to context switch.

front: Can processes interact, and what are the mechanisms called?
back: Yes. Mechanisms that let processes talk to one another are called inter-process communication (IPC).

front: Give the example used to motivate IPC.
back: A web application: a web server running in one process and a database running in another.

front: How does the OS isolate processes from one another?
back: Separate address spaces, controlled CPU allocation, and memory one process cannot reach from another.

front: What must IPC mechanisms do, and why must they be flexible and performant?
back: Transfer data between address spaces while maintaining protection and isolation. Interactions vary widely: periodic exchanges, continuous streams, or several processes coordinating on one shared piece of information.

front: Message passing IPC: how do processes communicate?
back: The OS establishes a communication channel (e.g. a shared buffer). One process writes/sends through it; the other reads/recvs from it. The sender explicitly puts information into a message.

front: What is the main benefit of message passing IPC?
back: The OS manages the channel and provides the same APIs (same system calls) to both sides for write/send and read/recv, so neither process implements the protocol itself.

front: What is the main downside of message passing IPC?
back: Overhead: every piece of information is copied from the sender's address space into kernel memory, then into the receiver's address space.

front: Diagram message passing IPC through an OS-managed channel.
Shared memory IPC: how do processes communicate?
back: The OS establishes a shared memory channel and maps it into both processes' address spaces. The processes read/write it directly, as they would any of their own memory.

front: What is the main benefit of shared memory IPC?
back: The OS is out of the fast path: it is not involved in individual exchanges, so processes incur no OS overhead on each read and write.

front: Shared memory IPC: when does it win over message passing, given setup cost?
back: Mapping memory between two address spaces is expensive, so shared memory only wins if that one-time setup is amortized across enough messages. For few exchanges, message passing can be better.

front: What is the disadvantage of shared memory IPC?
back: Because the OS is out of the way, APIs taken for granted in message passing must be reimplemented; without a fixed, well-defined API, the code tends to be more error-prone.

front: Diagram shared memory IPC mapped into both address spaces.
